subject: Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013)
object: Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) sequenced the exomes of 264 probands with infantile spasms or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and their parents. They identified a de novo mutation in the GABRB1 gene in one patient. The supplied text does not specify the variant or the patient's phenotype. This was one of six de novo mutations affecting subunits of the GABA-A receptor; the other five were four in GABRB3 and one in GABRA1. The authors suggested that rare mutations in different genes may converge on shared pathways.

Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013)
object: Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) studied patients from the Epilepsy Phenome/Genome Project with infantile spasms (n = 149) or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (n = 115). Patients with infantile spasms were required to have hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Patients with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome were required to have a slow or disorganized EEG background with generalized spike-and-wave activity or generalized paroxysmal fast activity. All patients had brain MRI or CT read as normal, mild diffuse atrophy or focal cortical dysplasia. None had moderate-to-severe developmental impairment before seizure onset.

subject: Janve et al. (2016)
object: Janve et al. (2016) studied a de novo heterozygous F246S mutation in the GABRB1 gene, which the Epi4K Consortium had found in a child with infantile spasms. F246 is a residue that is the same in all GABA-A receptor subunits and lies in transmembrane domain 1. When expressed with alpha-1 and gamma-2L subunits in HEK293T cells, the mutation reduced GABA-evoked peak current density by 25% in the homozygous condition and had no effect in the heterozygous condition. It slowed current deactivation. The authors concluded that the mutation impaired GABA-A receptor function and suggested that GABRB1 is a candidate human epilepsy gene.

subject: Janve et al. (2016)
object: In single-channel recordings, Janve et al. (2016) found that receptors with the GABRB1 F246S mutation had normal open probability despite a lower opening frequency. The mutation produced a gain of function, with about 3.75-fold longer mean open time and about 3.2-fold longer burst duration. It also lowered single-channel conductance to about 21 pS. The authors proposed that faster rise time and slower deactivation would lengthen inhibitory postsynaptic currents but would reduce charge transfer during later currents, resulting in a net loss of GABAergic inhibition.

subject: Janve et al. (2016)
object: Janve et al. (2016) found that the GABRB1 F246S mutation raised whole-cell holding currents about 5-fold in the homozygous condition, and these currents were partly blocked by zinc. In the absence of GABA, it increased spontaneous single-channel open probability 4-fold. Surface levels of the mutant beta-1 subunit were slightly but significantly lower, while total levels were unchanged. The authors suggested that receptors containing the mutant subunit opened spontaneously. Structural modeling predicted rearrangements in the coupling zone that spread to the transmembrane domains.

subject: Lien et al. (2016)
object: Lien et al. (2016) reported a second patient with epileptic encephalopathy who carried a de novo mutation in the GABRB1 gene.

subject: Burgess et al. (2019)
object: In a patient (Patient 63) with epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS), Burgess et al. (2019) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a de novo heterozygous variant in GABRB1 (chr4:47405633T>C, GRCh37), predicted to cause an ile247-to-thr (I247T) substitution. The variant was not found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. SIFT predicted it to be deleterious, PolyPhen predicted it to be benign, and it was classified as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria. The authors described GABRB1 as a new EIMFS gene that had previously been reported in other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.

subject: Burgess et al. (2019)
object: Burgess et al. (2019) reported a patient with a de novo GABRB1 variant who was studied at age 2 years. The patient had focal seizures beginning at 4 months, with interhemispheric seizure migration (an inclusion criterion of the cohort). The patient also had profound to severe developmental impairment and hypotonia, and did not have epileptic spasms or microcephaly.

subject: Burgess et al. (2019)
object: Burgess et al. (2019) found causative variants in 93 of 135 patients with EIMFS (69%), spread across 23 genes. Nine of these genes were new to EIMFS, among them GABRA1 and GABRB1. The authors emphasized the role of GABA-related mechanisms and noted that 3 patients carried variants in the known EIMFS gene GABRB3.
